title: Ask disabled people early
fact: Accessibility reports and usability feedback reveal barriers that guidelines and automated checks can miss.
action: Invite a disabled user or contributor into one design or testing conversation.

title: Publish an accessibility promise
fact: A short accessibility statement tells users what you support, what limits exist, and how to report barriers.
action: Add an ACCESSIBILITY.md file and link it from your README.

title: Give accessibility reports their own path
fact: A dedicated label and template can collect assistive technology, environment, severity, and reproduction details.
action: Create an accessibility issue template with fields for the user's tools, expected behavior, and actual behavior.

title: Build readable documentation
fact: Logical headings, descriptive links, plain language, and real lists make documentation easier to navigate with assistive technology.
action: Scan one document for skipped headings, vague link text, and manually typed lists.

title: Describe non-text content
fact: Images, diagrams, and videos need text alternatives, captions, or transcripts so their information is not locked to one format.
action: Add useful alt text to one image and a transcript or captions to your most-watched video.

title: Make keyboard use a requirement
fact: Interactive controls should be reachable by keyboard, show focus clearly, and follow a logical tab order.
action: Complete your main user flow without a mouse and record the first place where focus gets lost.

title: Prefer native controls
fact: Native HTML controls provide keyboard behavior, focus handling, and screen reader semantics that custom controls must recreate.
action: Replace one custom button, input, or menu with its native equivalent if the native control fits.

title: Do not make color do all the work
fact: Color should not be the only signal for status or errors, and text and controls need adequate contrast.
action: Find one color-only status indicator and add a text label, icon, or other redundant signal.

title: Give CLI users usable output
fact: Clear help, machine-readable output, text labels, and standard exit codes make command-line tools easier to use and script.
action: Add a concrete example to --help and a --json or equivalent output mode to one command.

title: Test accessibility in two ways
fact: Automated checks catch common regressions, while keyboard and screen reader passes expose problems automation cannot judge.
action: Add an accessibility smoke test to your release checklist and run it with keyboard-only navigation.

title: Make accessibility part of done
fact: Accessibility is easier to maintain when feature and bug-fix acceptance criteria include it before implementation starts.
action: Add keyboard, focus, labels, and reduced-motion checks to your UI pull request checklist.

title: Require MFA for privileged access
fact: Multi-factor authentication adds a second barrier when an attacker gets a privileged contributor's password.
action: List administrators and maintainers, then verify that every privileged account has MFA enabled.

title: Scan code before it ships
fact: Static analysis can find security flaws before runtime and can run in builds or code review.
action: Choose a SAST tool for your languages and run it on every pull request, starting with a small rule set.

title: Keep secrets out of commits
fact: Secret scanning can catch exposed API keys, tokens, and passwords before or after they reach a remote repository.
action: Enable secret scanning or a pre-push check, and rehearse how you will revoke a leaked credential.

title: Automate dependency updates
fact: Software composition tools can match dependencies to known vulnerabilities and open updates for safer versions.
action: Enable Dependabot, Renovate, or an equivalent tool and reserve time to review its pull requests.

title: Inventory license risk
fact: An SBOM and automated license checks show which components and license terms enter your software supply chain.
action: Generate an SBOM for one release and flag dependencies whose licenses need a legal review.

title: Protect important branches
fact: Branch protection can require review and passing status checks before changes reach a main branch.
action: Require review and successful CI before merging to your default branch.

title: Publish a private security route
fact: A SECURITY.md file and private reporting channel reduce the chance that a vulnerability is disclosed before it can be fixed.
action: Add SECURITY.md with a reporting address, expected response time, and disclosure guidance.

title: Write down your threat model
fact: A lightweight threat model tells users and researchers what the project trusts, protects, and considers in scope.
action: Document your assets, trust boundaries, likely misuse, and out-of-scope reports beside your security policy.

title: Prepare an incident checklist
fact: A small response plan clarifies who triages reports, evaluates severity, coordinates a fix, and notifies affected users.
action: Write a four-step incident checklist and link it from SECURITY.md.

title: Make security a shared job
fact: Clear roles, least-privilege access, education, and upstream coordination keep security from depending on one person.
action: Assign owners for vulnerability reports, dependency updates, and security patches, then review access.

title: Know what energizes your maintenance
fact: Naming the parts of open source work that energize you helps you prioritize work you can sustain.
action: Write down two maintenance tasks that give you energy and protect time for one of them this week.

title: Name your sources of stress
fact: Low feedback, too many commitments, isolation, scarce resources, and conflicting demands can all push maintainers out of balance.
action: Mark the biggest current stressor and choose one boundary or support request that addresses it.

title: Check whether your pace is sustainable
fact: A pace that works for a week may not work for ten weeks, ten months, or ten years.
action: Use a burnout checklist or your own weekly notes to spot one pattern that needs changing.

title: Delegate before you disappear
fact: More contributors and more than one project contact make it possible to take a break without abandoning users.
action: Ask one trusted contributor to own a small area and document how they can make decisions there.

title: Find maintainer peers
fact: Other maintainers can provide practical support, perspective, and ideas for handling recurring project pressure.
action: Join one maintainer group or schedule a candid conversation with someone who runs a similar project.

title: Treat funding as a support tool
fact: Sponsorships, grants, and other funding can buy back time for maintainers who cannot afford to volunteer it.
action: Add a funding option to your project or research one program whose requirements match your work.

title: Automate the boring work
fact: Automation can remove routine tasks and leave maintainers more time for judgment, support, and creative work.
action: Automate one repetitive check or notification with a script, bot, or CI job.

title: Put rest on the calendar
fact: Regular breaks and explicit availability boundaries help maintainers keep contributing without turning a project into constant work.
action: Choose a no-maintenance block this week and tell the community when you will be unavailable.

title: Code is not the only contribution
fact: Documentation, design, events, triage, moderation, and mentoring can fill gaps that code alone does not address.
action: Pick one non-code task in a project you use and make a small contribution.

title: Contribute from your strengths
fact: Open source projects need writers, designers, organizers, reviewers, and helpers as well as programmers.
action: Search a project's issues for a task matching a skill you already have.

title: Documentation is real project work
fact: Examples, tutorials, translations, and clearer existing docs can help users and reduce repeated support questions.
action: Improve one confusing paragraph or add a small example to a project you use.

title: Read the project's map
fact: Roles, repository files, issue trackers, pull requests, and discussion channels reveal how a project actually works.
action: Find the README, LICENSE, contribution guide, code of conduct, and main discussion channel before proposing work.

title: Use the contribute page
fact: On GitHub, adding /contribute to a repository URL surfaces issues that are intended as beginner-friendly starting points.
action: Open the /contribute page for a project you use and shortlist one small issue.

title: Check a project before investing
fact: Recent activity, open issues, pull requests, and respectful responses are clues that a project can receive your work.
action: Review a project's recent commits and a few issue or pull request discussions before starting.

title: Give every request context
fact: A useful issue or question explains what you tried, what happened, and why the proposed change would help the project.
action: Rewrite your next issue to include a minimal reproduction and the result you expected.

title: Search before you ask
fact: A quick pass through docs, open and closed issues, and project discussions often answers a question or reveals existing context.
action: Search the repository and web for your idea before opening a new issue.

title: Keep contribution requests short
fact: Concise requests are easier for busy maintainers to understand and review.
action: Put the problem, proposed change, and next step in the first few sentences of your request.

title: Keep ordinary project talk public
fact: Public discussions let future contributors learn from the exchange and keep maintainers from answering the same question privately.
action: Move your next non-sensitive support question to the project's issue tracker or discussion channel.

title: Claim an issue before working
fact: A short comment can prevent duplicate work and tells maintainers who is exploring a solution.
action: Comment on an issue with your intended approach before you start a non-trivial fix.

title: Open a draft early
fact: An early draft pull request lets maintainers react to direction and scope before you spend weeks polishing the wrong change.
action: Open a draft pull request when you have a rough path and list the questions you want reviewed.

title: Test and follow local style
fact: Passing tests and matching project conventions reduce the review work required to merge a contribution.
action: Run the documented test command and compare your changes with the project's formatting and review norms.

title: Follow up once, in public
fact: If a contribution has had no response for more than a week, a polite reminder in the same thread is reasonable.
action: Post one concise public follow-up, then choose another project or task if nobody responds.

title: Respond to requested changes
fact: Review comments are part of collaboration, so contributors should either make the changes or tell the maintainer they are stepping away.
action: Reply to every requested change with an update, a question, or a clear handoff.

title: A rejection can become a fork
fact: Maintainers may decline a contribution for scope or design reasons, and a fork gives you room to pursue a different direction.
action: Ask for specific feedback, thank the reviewer, and fork only if the difference still matters to you.

title: Define open source in your own words
fact: An open source license gives people permission to use, study, modify, and distribute a project.
action: Read your project's license and write one sentence explaining what it permits users to do.

title: Free is not the same as free of charge
fact: In open source, free and libre describe user freedoms; price is a separate choice.
action: Use your README and pricing page to state both the license freedoms and any paid services clearly.

title: Write down why you are opening the project
fact: Clear goals help a maintainer decide what to accept, what to decline, and where help is needed.
action: Add a short goals or vision section to your README before announcing the project.

title: Budget the work beyond code
fact: Issues, reviews, documentation, and project promotion continue after launch and need an owner and time.
action: Name who will handle maintenance after launch and reserve a weekly amount of time for it.

title: Launch when feedback is welcome
fact: There is no required project stage for going open; the useful threshold is being ready for others to inspect and discuss it.
action: Choose a small public milestone and state what kind of feedback you want when you publish it.

title: Ship the four project basics
fact: A license, README, contribution guide, and code of conduct set expectations for users and contributors.
action: Put LICENSE, README, CONTRIBUTING, and CODE_OF_CONDUCT files in your repository root.

title: Choose a standard license
fact: An established license protects reuse and is easier for users to understand than custom terms.
action: Compare MIT, Apache-2.0, GPLv3, and other options at choosealicense.com before publishing.

title: Make the README answer four questions
fact: A useful README explains what the project does, why it matters, how to start, and where to get help.
action: Ask a new reader to find all four answers without opening another file, then fix the first gap.

title: Put the contribution path in writing
fact: Contributing guidelines can explain bug reports, feature requests, setup, tests, and the kinds of help you want.
action: Create CONTRIBUTING.md with one tested setup path and one example of a welcome contribution.

title: Adopt a code of conduct early
fact: A code of conduct defines who is covered, where it applies, how to report a violation, and what happens next.
action: Add a CODE_OF_CONDUCT file and link it from your README and contribution guide.

title: Choose a name that explains the project
fact: A memorable name that hints at what a project does gives potential users useful context before they click.
action: Ask someone unfamiliar with the project what they expect it to do from its name alone.

title: Check names before you announce
fact: Similar projects, unavailable handles, search results, and trademarks can create confusion or legal trouble later.
action: Search your proposed name across its ecosystem, reserve the needed handles, and check the WIPO database.

title: Let your writing set the tone
fact: README text, issue replies, and code style teach people what kind of community your project expects.
action: Rewrite one terse or exclusionary sentence in your docs with simple, welcoming language.

title: State the problem before promoting
fact: People become users or contributors when a project solves a problem for them, so its message should start there.
action: Complete the sentence: this project helps X do Y, then use that sentence in your README opening.

title: Give the project one home
fact: A single URL or namespace makes a project easier to remember, follow, and share.
action: Choose one canonical project URL and link every profile, talk, and announcement to it.

title: Show the project in use
fact: A simple website, tutorial, or example gives prospective users a route from discovery to trying the project.
action: Publish one small example that shows the project's result, not just its installation command.

title: Find the right online audience
fact: Targeted communities are more useful than broad promotion because they contain people who already have the problem you solve.
action: Choose one relevant forum or project community and contribute a helpful answer before mentioning your project.

title: Help before you promote
fact: Context and useful answers stand out better than posting the same project link everywhere.
action: Answer one relevant question in full and mention your project only if it genuinely solves that person's problem.

title: Tailor a talk to its audience
fact: Meetups and conferences work better when a talk explains the value and examples that matter to that particular audience.
action: Pick one local or ecosystem event and rewrite your talk abstract around its attendees' needs.

title: Build reputation by helping others
fact: Thoughtful contributions to other projects give people context for your work and build trust over time.
action: Make one useful contribution to a related project before asking its community to share yours.

title: Reduce friction at every contributor step
fact: A welcoming project helps people move from user to contributor by making each next step clear and achievable.
action: Walk through your project as a new user and remove the first confusing step you encounter.

title: Keep beginner work visible
fact: Good first issue and documentation labels help casual contributors find work that matches their experience.
action: Label one small issue with enough context that a newcomer can start without private coaching.

title: Thank the first contact
fact: A quick, positive response to a new issue or pull request can determine whether someone returns to the project.
action: Reply to your newest contributor with thanks and one clear next step.

title: Document decisions in public
fact: Public roadmaps, meeting notes, review processes, and decision records let newcomers participate with the same context as regulars.
action: Post the takeaway from your next maintainer meeting in an issue or discussion thread.

title: Acknowledge requests quickly
fact: Even when a full review must wait, an early acknowledgement tells contributors that their request entered the conversation.
action: Set a reminder to acknowledge new issues and pull requests within the response time you publish.

title: Give the community a public room
fact: A public issue tracker, forum, or chat archive helps people learn from one another and keeps support from filling a maintainer's inbox.
action: Choose one primary public channel and redirect the next non-sensitive private support request there.

title: Keep sensitive reports private
fact: Security issues and serious code of conduct violations need a private reporting route even when normal project talk is public.
action: Test the private contact listed in SECURITY.md or your code of conduct before someone needs it.

title: Do not tolerate harmful behavior
fact: Unchecked bullying and hostile debate can drive away helpful community members who never complain publicly.
action: Name the behavior, point to the community rule, and act consistently when a discussion becomes harmful.

title: Meet casual contributors where they are
fact: People who contribute occasionally need enough setup and context to make progress without learning the entire project first.
action: Add a short newcomer section to CONTRIBUTING.md and link to a first, low-risk task.

title: Share ownership deliberately
fact: Credit, responsibility, and a path to leadership give contributors reasons to keep investing in a project.
action: Add a CONTRIBUTORS file or invite a regular contributor to own a clearly bounded area.

title: Use an organization and backup admin
fact: Shared account ownership protects a project from depending on one personal account or maintainer.
action: Move a growing project to an organization and add a trusted backup administrator.

title: Facilitate conflict instead of joining it
fact: A maintainer who sets a calm example and keeps people respectful can stop a difficult discussion from escalating.
action: In the next heated thread, restate the issue neutrally and ask what information is still needed.

title: Seek consensus before voting
fact: A consensus-seeking process prioritizes hearing serious concerns before moving forward instead of reducing the discussion to a tally.
action: Before a major vote, summarize each unresolved concern and ask what would address it.

title: Turn arguments into next steps
fact: A discussion is useful when it moves toward a decision; asking what happens next can pull a thread back from personal debate.
action: Add a concrete next action and owner to the next stalled project discussion.

title: Choose a tiebreaker in advance
fact: A documented tiebreaker gives a project a last resort when a respectful discussion cannot resolve a major disagreement.
action: Add the decision owner and escalation process to GOVERNANCE.md before the next dispute.

title: Remember that maintenance is more than code
fact: As a project grows, responding to users, reviewing changes, and organizing the community can take more time than writing code.
action: List your recurring maintenance tasks and mark which ones need an owner or a documented process.

title: Write down the project's vision
fact: A public vision helps a maintainer filter requests and resist scope creep.
action: Add a short vision and a list of out-of-scope requests to your README or VISION file.

title: Publish realistic expectations
fact: Response times, accepted contribution types, review rules, and available hours tell people what the maintainer can actually sustain.
action: Add your expected response window and weekly availability to the contribution guide.

title: Record private decisions publicly
fact: Publishing notes from maintainer conversations gives new community members access to decisions that would otherwise become hidden history.
action: Summarize the next private planning conversation in a public issue or decision record.

title: Say no by pointing to scope
fact: A documented project criterion makes a refusal about the work's fit instead of a judgment about the person proposing it.
action: Link your vision when declining the next out-of-scope request and suggest a better place for it if one exists.

title: Close unwanted work kindly
fact: Thanking a contributor, explaining the mismatch, and closing promptly is kinder than leaving an unwanted issue or pull request unanswered.
action: Resolve one stale request with a brief explanation and a link to the relevant project rule.

title: Ask for context before the code
fact: Issue and pull request templates can require enough information to prevent work that the project cannot accept.
action: Add a template asking for motivation, scope, tests, and a link to any prior discussion.

title: Turn repeated corrections into mentoring
fact: An enthusiastic contributor who misses project expectations may need a smaller task, clearer explanation, or a mentor.
action: Offer one well-scoped starter issue to a contributor whose first attempt needs more guidance.

title: Share the easy work
fact: Delegating approachable issues and recognizing repeated contributions grows the set of people who can help maintain the project.
action: Leave one non-critical, well-defined issue for a contributor instead of fixing it yourself.

title: Use extensions for different needs
fact: A fork, plugin, API, or customization hook can serve a valid use case without forcing every project user into one vision.
action: Identify one stable extension point that would let users solve needs outside your core scope.

title: Let tests guard the merge
fact: Required automated tests give contributors confidence and stop regressions before a change reaches the main branch.
action: Run your test suite on every pull request and require its status check before merging.

title: Automate routine maintenance
fact: Release tools, dependency updates, issue templates, and stale-request handling can remove repetitive maintainer work.
action: Automate one recurring task, then document the escape hatch for unusual cases.

title: Pause before burnout decides
fact: A planned break is healthier than waiting until a backlog and dread force an abrupt stop.
action: Set a maintenance pause, announce the dates, and point users to the best available support.

title: Recognize broad forms of leadership
fact: Maintainers and contributors can earn leadership roles through documentation, triage, events, or community work as well as code.
action: Write down what your project means by contributor, maintainer, and committer.

title: Make leadership visible
fact: A team page, README section, or CONTRIBUTORS file tells the community who owns which responsibilities.
action: Publish current project roles and one way to contact each responsibility area.

title: Document the path to leadership
fact: A clear process for joining a core team or subcommittee makes leadership feel earned and open rather than private.
action: Add criteria and a nomination or review process for maintainers to GOVERNANCE.md.

title: Grant access with guardrails
fact: Commit access can build ownership, while protected branches limit the damage of an accidental or unreviewed change.
action: Define when someone earns write access and keep review and CI requirements on important branches.

title: Pick governance for your context
fact: BDFL, merit-based, and liberal contribution models make different tradeoffs around authority, history, and consensus.
action: Name your current decision model and one reason it fits the project's size and community.

title: Let governance grow with the community
fact: Early expectations can be documented at launch, while more formal governance can follow once community dynamics are visible.
action: Write down the decisions you already make and schedule a governance review after your next growth milestone.

title: Judge paid contributions on the work
fact: Commercial use and paid developers are compatible with open source; contributions should be evaluated on their technical and community merits.
action: Review a proposal against your published criteria without asking whether the contributor is paid.

title: Do not form a legal entity by default
fact: A project usually does not need a separate legal entity unless it handles money, and a fiscal sponsor can be an alternative for donations.
action: Before incorporating, list the money, contracts, and liability needs that a legal entity would address.

title: Volunteering is not the only model
fact: Some people contribute for learning or community, while sustained maintenance may require paid time for others.
action: Ask what work your project needs and whether the current unpaid arrangement excludes people who could do it.

title: Pitch open source work to your employer
fact: An employer may support maintenance when it improves a product, recruiting, reputation, or the wider ecosystem it relies on.
action: Write a one-page proposal connecting your open source work to a concrete employer benefit.

title: Keep company and community interests clear
fact: Company funding can support open source, but community decisions should not quietly become company-only decisions.
action: Document who funds your work, who makes project decisions, and how outside contributors participate.

title: Try more than one funding route
fact: Sponsors, crowdfunding, bounties, grants, and employer support fit different kinds of projects and audiences.
action: Compare two funding routes against your audience, time, and administrative capacity before choosing one.

title: Budget project funding honestly
fact: Project funding may pay contributors, hosting, or new features, so the request should name the work it will support.
action: List the next three project costs and connect each one to a specific outcome.

title: Match sponsorship to an audience
fact: Sponsorship tends to work best when a project already has a visible audience or a strong reputation.
action: Gather usage stories and a clear sponsorship ask before contacting potential backers.

title: Consider paid services around open source
fact: Support, hosted offerings, and additional features can fund a project while the core software remains open source.
action: Identify one service users already request and test whether a paid version could support maintenance.

title: Write grants around outcomes
fact: Grants can support individuals or projects, but each funder has its own eligibility and reporting requirements.
action: Find one relevant grant and write down its eligibility, deadline, deliverables, and reporting obligations.

title: Prove the project matters
fact: A funding case is stronger when it combines impact, adoption evidence, value to the funder, and a specific use of funds.
action: Collect one metric, one user story, and one concrete milestone for your next funding request.

title: Explain how money will arrive
fact: Funders may require a nonprofit, fiscal sponsor, or individual contractor, so receiving funds is part of the proposal.
action: Confirm the recipient and payment requirements before promising a funded project milestone.

title: Use a code of conduct to set expectations
fact: A code of conduct defines behavior standards and gives maintainers a basis for addressing harmful interactions.
action: Choose a code of conduct and make its scope visible to every project participant.

title: Define where the code applies
fact: A useful code of conduct says which spaces and activities it covers, who it covers, and how violations are reported.
action: List your repository, chat, events, and sponsor spaces in the scope section of the policy.

title: Use prior art for conduct rules
fact: Established texts such as the Contributor Covenant can save a project from inventing unclear behavioral rules from scratch.
action: Adopt a recognized code, adapt only what you understand, and link it from README and CONTRIBUTING.md.

title: Plan enforcement before the incident
fact: A private reporting route, named recipients, and an alternate contact show that the policy can be acted on fairly.
action: Test a report to the listed contact and add a fallback for reports involving that person.

title: Investigate reports with context
fact: Review the report seriously and gather surrounding conversations and perspectives before deciding what happened.
action: Create a private incident checklist that separates evidence gathering from the final response.

title: Protect the person who reports
fact: The maintainer, not the reporter, should handle direct contact with the person accused unless the reporter asks for another arrangement.
action: Write down who will communicate with the accused and how reporter consent and confidentiality are handled.

title: Apply standards consistently
fact: Maintainers owe each report a fair review and should address harmful behavior even when it falls just outside the written policy.
action: After resolving a report, note whether the policy needs a clearer example or rule.

title: Measure what serves your goal
fact: Metrics help with decisions, but popularity is not automatically the right measure for every open source project.
action: Write the decision a metric should inform before adding another dashboard or counter.

title: Track how people discover the project
fact: Page views, unique visitors, referrers, and popular pages show whether people can find the project and what catches their attention.
action: Review your project's traffic sources and record one channel worth investing in.

title: Treat downloads as a baseline
fact: Package downloads and clone counts can show change over time, but they do not necessarily equal installs or active use.
action: Choose one usage measure, document what it counts, and avoid presenting it as a user total.

title: Compare discovery with usage
fact: High traffic with low use may mean the project is hard to adopt or is reaching the wrong audience.
action: Compare a discovery channel with its activation step and ask one new user where they stopped.

title: Watch contributor retention
fact: New, casual, and repeat contributors reveal whether a project is gaining people who return, not only people who try it once.
action: Track first-time and repeat contributors separately for the next release cycle.

title: Use backlog size as a signal
fact: Open issue and pull request counts can reveal when triage or review volume is exceeding maintainer capacity.
action: Set a monthly backlog review and identify the oldest item that needs a decision.

title: Measure response time
fact: A quick acknowledgement can keep a contributor engaged even when a full review will take longer.
action: Record the time to first response for issues and pull requests during one month.

title: Choose community health measures
fact: The useful metric is the one that focuses attention on behavior your project wants to encourage, not the one with the biggest number.
action: Remove one metric nobody uses to make a decision and replace it with a question the team needs answered.

title: Copyright starts with the author
fact: Creative work is normally protected by default, so others need an explicit license to use, copy, modify, or distribute it.
action: Add a clear license before inviting others to reuse or contribute to your project.

title: Public does not mean open source
fact: A public GitHub repository can be viewed and forked under GitHub's terms, but it does not grant broad reuse permissions by itself.
action: Check that your public repository includes the intended license file and copyright information.

title: Prefer a known license
fact: Standard licenses give users a shared set of permissions and conditions that are easier to understand than custom terms.
action: Use choosealicense.com to compare standard options instead of writing a new license from scratch.

title: Check dependency compatibility
fact: Your project's license must account for the conditions attached to the libraries and other code it distributes.
action: Make a list of direct dependencies and record each license before choosing your project's license.

title: Separate copyleft from source available
fact: Copyleft licenses have sharing conditions, while source-available licenses can add business restrictions and may not meet the open source definition.
action: Flag GPL, AGPL, MPL, LGPL, BSL, and SSPL dependencies for a deliberate compatibility review.

title: License non-code assets too
fact: Images, icons, videos, fonts, data, and other bundled materials can carry different license terms from the source code.
action: Add a third-party notices inventory for non-code assets in your next release.

title: Treat relicensing as governance
fact: Changing a license can affect compatibility, contributors, users, and the project's future direction, so it needs clear consultation.
action: Open a public discussion and consult qualified legal counsel before planning a license change.

title: Find every copyright holder
fact: A license change may require agreement from contributors or their employers, and a commit history is only a starting point for finding them.
action: Map contributors and employer ownership before asking for consent to relicense an established project.

title: Do not add a CLA by reflex
fact: An open source license often supplies the inbound and outbound permissions a project needs, while an extra agreement adds administration.
action: Write down the exact legal need a contributor agreement solves before requiring one.

title: Audit third-party material
fact: Company projects need to account for third-party code, trade secrets, patents, trademarks, privacy, and dependency license conditions.
action: Ask legal and engineering to review third-party notices, secrets, names, data collection, and patent timing before release.

title: Keep a licensing record
fact: A current record of licenses for components, subcomponents, and dependencies makes compliance work easier to repeat.
action: Store dependency versions, licenses, notices, and SBOM output with each release record.
